[h2]Grand Theft Auto V Steam Review[/h2]
[b]Rating:[/b] 🟢 [b]Recommended[/b]
[hr][/hr]
[h3]The Ultimate Nostalgia Trip, But Make It 60 FPS[/h3]
If you had told me back in 2013, huddled over a humming, overheating PlayStation 3 with the original dualshock clacking away, that I would one day be cruising down the Vinewood Hills at a buttery-smooth 60 frames per second on Steam, I probably would have cried.

Back on the PS3, GTA V was a technical marvel. We all stared in awe at the sun setting over Los Santos, forgiving the occasional texture pop-in, the 30 FPS drops during massive explosions, and the agonizingly long loading screens where you could easily go make a sandwich while Trevor was loading in. It was a masterpiece of its generation.

Fast forward to playing it on Steam, and it feels like meeting an old friend who just got a massive glow-up.

[h3]What’s Better on Steam?[/h3]
[list]
[] [b]Performance & Fidelity:[/b] Going from the console versions of the past to a modern PC setup is night and day. The draw distances, the crisp 1080p/4K resolution, and the fluid frame rates breathe entirely new life into a world I thought I knew by heart.
[] [b]Mods & Customization:[/b] While the vanilla game is fantastic, the PC modding community is the real MVP. Whether it's graphical overhauls, quality-of-life tweaks, or just messing around, it adds endless replay value.
[*] [b]Seamless Convenience:[/b] Having it right in your Steam library alongside your achievements, screenshots, and friends list makes jumping back into Los Santos effortless.
[/list]

[h3]The Verdict[/h3]
Coming back to this game after years away feels weirdly comforting. Sure, the radio ads are permanently burned into my brain, and I can still navigate the map blindfolded, but the charm hasn't faded one bit. Michael, Franklin, and Trevor are just as chaotic and entertaining as they were a decade ago.

If you’re on the fence about double-dipping or jumping over from the old console days, do it. It’s a nostalgic masterpiece that still holds its own, and experiencing it without the hardware limitations of 2013 is the ultimate way to play.

[i]Ah ♥♥♥♥, here we go again.[/i] 🎮🔥

Greatest Game of the 2020's. I am an old Bauldur's Gate veteran, and to be honest, I was afraid to try this one. It looked very different than 1 and 2 from the images with all of its new-fangled, 3d, fancy graphics. And from what I saw in videos and trailers, it just kinda looked like a dirty sex game. I was terrified to try it becasue I didn't want it to ruin my fond memories. But there was one Steam review that helped my confidence. It pointed out that this game is ALL about choice. The review amusingly stated, "You don't have to ♥♥♥♥ the bear." LOL. So I bit the bullet and bought it. 
And boy am I glad.
Even on the character creation screen it was drawing me into the fantasy with its beautiful music. When the story started, I found that I liked Lae'zel. I liked Shadowheart. I could see that the writing and voice acting was decent, and I could see how those two didn't get along. I even liked Astarion when I met him—and I had even previously HATED the way he looked when no one would shut up about him on Youtube. I thought he looked like a sleazy Vegas magician lol. But It was all fine. 
I found that nothing bothered me as I played. The story held my attention—which is really saying something because I have been a BRUTAL writing critic ever since I became a writer lol. This game's story has my approval.
Yes, it's all very choice oriented, and that was a great thing. When there's various sex scenes getting isolated and showcased around the net, that would make any game look like a "dirty sex game" lol. So it's cool. I was able to play the narrative I wanted to see for my particular character.
Earlier, I mentioned that I was worried it wouldn't "feel" like Bauldur's Gate. Well turns out it did. Even though the graphics were heavily upgraded, it did still oddly feel like a continuation of the old games. I even feel like some of the old item-oriented sound effects were original. Not sure though.
Best of all was the battle system. Early on, I got to this one area that had a large party of enemies inside a building and it was very hard (I played on Tactician for my first play through because of my Bauldur's Gate history). It was SO hard, though, and I kept dying... And I noticed that I was hooked. I was determined to beat that battle and it was invigorating. I just loved the challenge! Too bad it will probably be a while before the next one comes out. DX.
This game put me through SUCH emotion though! I cried at the end. I cried at something at the middle too. This game really knew how to mess with me lol. Even when I came back to its Steam page, seeing the trailers made me feel something. ;_;
I ADORE the soundtrack, btw! I've been singing those songs and relistening to them on Youtube ever since that first day in the character creator lol.
It's just wonderful. This game blew me away. Thank you, Larian. I really needed that escape.

comment:
Grand Theft Auto V is not just a video game; it is a monumental cultural phenomenon and a sprawling, technicolor mirror held up to the face of modern capitalism. From the moment you step into the sun-drenched, smog-choked streets of Los Santos, Rockstar Games delivers a masterclass in open-world design, storytelling, and social commentary. It captures the chaotic essence of the American Dream, chews it up, and spits it back out in a glorious explosion of high-speed chases, bullet-riddled bank heists, and dark, unfiltered humor.
At the beating heart of this epic narrative is the franchise’s most ambitious storytelling mechanic: the three-protagonist system. By weaving together the lives of three distinct criminals, the game offers a multi-layered perspective of a deeply flawed world. There is Michael, a retired bank robber trapped in a toxic, wealthy suburban nightmare, suffocated by the boredom of his own success. Then there is Franklin, a young, ambitious street hustler trying to escape the cycle of the ghetto by climbing the ladder of organized crime. And finally, Trevor, a volatile, unhinged, and borderline psychotic meth-dealer who embodies the absolute, chaotic id of the GTA franchise itself. The ability to seamlessly switch between these characters creates a dynamic, cinematic rhythm where a tranquil day at a luxury mansion can instantly dissolve into a chaotic desert shootout.
The true star of the show, however, is the map of San Andreas itself. The attention to detail is staggering. Los Santos feels alive, reacting dynamically to the player's presence. Pedestrians yell on their cell phones, traffic clogs the freeways at rush hour, and the neon lights of Vinewood reflect beautifully off the hoods of stolen supercars. Whether you are planning a meticulously detailed, multi-stage heist, diving into the ocean depths, hijacking a military fighter jet, or simply driving down Del Perro Beach while listening to a satirical talk-radio station, the level of player freedom remains completely unmatched.
Ultimately, Grand Theft Auto V stands as a timeless masterpiece because it doesn’t just let you play in a world; it forces you to experience its madness. It is a brilliant, cynical, and wildly entertaining critique of celebrity culture, government corruption, and consumerism. Decades from now, when historians look back at how video games evolved into the definitive art form of the 21st century, GTA V will undoubtedly stand tall as the pinnacle of interactive entertainment.

Title: A Masterpiece… but Missing One Simple Freedom

Baldur’s Gate 3 is easily one of the best RPGs ever made.
The world is rich, the characters are unforgettable, and the amount of freedom in quests and combat is incredible. Every fight feels tactical, every choice matters, and the replay value is huge. It’s a game that pulls you in and refuses to let go.

But there is one major limitation that holds it back for players like me:
you cannot freely customise your own full party.

For a game that celebrates freedom, it’s surprising that creating a full custom team is restricted. Many players enjoy building their own party of heroes — not because we dislike the companions, but because we love tactical synergy, role‑playing, and experimenting with different builds. Even creating just three custom characters makes the game harder, because the difficulty doesn’t scale down.

It feels like the game pushes you toward using Origin companions, even when you want to enjoy the story your own way.

Still, despite this limitation, BG3 remains an amazing experience.
The writing, combat, music, and world-building are top-tier.
I just hope that one day, Larian gives players the option to create a full custom party without workarounds.

A game this good deserves that extra freedom.

i haven't finished this game and i probably won't, i doubt it will end in any way that satisfies me.

story-wise the game is better than most videogames, but that's not exactly stiff competition.
the celebrity actor is interesting and all but if you do side content then the writing for johnny goes downhill pretty fast. he changes from friendly to hating you and back with a real quickness. very jarring.
your romance options are mostly just eyecandy. i don't care about them at all and i tried to.
chemistry-wise there's only one of four characters that makes sense because she's relevant to the actual main story and one of the endings.

the original cyberpunk 2013 is a tabletop RPG series. you need a lot of worldbuilding written just to get off the ground, and the books are rich for what they are. something which gets better with some of the later editions.
however, none of that seems to translate through to 2077. this feels like a totally different world with some similar terms and figureheads. genre-wise it's more like post-cyberpunk instead of just cyberpunk. 
which means it's not really "punk"

gameplay-wise the game is just, fine.
it's sloppy in a lot of areas but the systems are interesting enough to carry through to the point where the story's momentum starts breaking down, presumably capable of lasting to the end of a better told story.

a lot of people seem to enjoy the game, but i can't recommend it, it's not cyberpunk.

comment:
Well, it's a CDProjektRed game. It has an interesting, visually distinctive, rich game world and the game is utterly contemptuous of the idea that anyone who is not a straight cis man might want to play in it. 

Let's start with the character creator. Your options are: burly man or petite sexy woman. There are more options for sexy woman than burly man. I came in wanting to make a butch woman, like my character in the TTRPG.  No. You cannot make butch, masc, curvy, fat, or even tall. You can adjust tit size. You can't make yourself or even your favorite singer.  You can make Harley Quinn. Oh. And you can give her a big or small penis. Hahahaha. She has a dong now.

So I gave up on that and decided to make a character who looks like someone from Skinny Puppy. You know, an actual goth punk. Nope. Can't do that, either. Face customization is...subtle, and the hair for men is universally tame. Oh yes. You can give him a vulva on his big burly body. 

There's really no roleplaying in the game either. There is one right answer to all dialog options and no responsiveness to different choices. Your V is just  not really customizable.

But,  I hear you arguing, you never really see your character in the game (you know, other than the times you see them naked or vulnerable), so why does it matter?  It matters in that I'm really not sure why they bothered. It's clear that the point of having female characters in this game is so the male player can leer at them, but you can't even play in 3rd person and stare at V's ass.  If there's no roleplaying and no flexibility on the character creator, why spend the resources on it at all?  Why not let people upload a bitmap portrait like in the old CRPGs? Why not lock the character as male like the Witcher. At least then there was an excuse for the ubiquitous misogyny in the game world because you were seeing it through Geralt's eyes and desires. I'm used to playing straight guys. I play video games. I'm not used to hearing hype about how inclusive a game is and finding out that it's inclusion as conceived by a fifteen year old boy, who thinks it's a joke.

And the game world is sexist. two thirds of the billboards in the game are some sort of sexy woman with her legs spread sucking on something. I'm stuck in a room with a holographic pole dancer with no head just tits and ass for one of the longer exposes at the beginning of the game. Half the characters talk to you like you're in a porno for no reason at all. Yes, I know this is a world inspired by Bladerunner and Total Recall and 80s punk aesthetic. The TTRPG world isn't like this, and even Bladerunner limited itself to one or two sexy billboards. Bladerunner's cyborg sex workers had curves and actual punk hair.

The game is fun enough, and the story is interesting, and I spent sixty bucks on it, so I'll sink some hours in it, but I won't be in love with it and I probably won't buy their next effort.

If you want to enjoy this fantasy as a woman, or a trans person, or really any of the stereotypically portrayed ethnic groups in the game, you should look ANYWHERE else.  Or,   just accept the fact that this is a game that is for straight guys and the game is aggressive about sending that message.

comment:
Sekiro was a groundbreaking experience for me, I was addicted to that game, so much so I had to force myself to stop playing it, even after completing all of the achievments, so I could go back to being a productive member of society (by which I mean, play other games on my to play-list, lol).
One thing that worried me though, was that Dark Souls 3, a game I played for over 400h and also completed, would feel stale by comparison, and that its combat system, which I once adored, would now seem boring.

Having played Eldern Ring for about 60h and coming close to finishing it (I only have the Elden Beast and Melania left) it seems I was right. This game, having drawn more from Dark Souls than Sekiro in terms of combat mechanic and enemy desgin, has completely truned me off any similar games in the series.
If whatever comes out of From Software next is closer to Elden Ring than it is to Sekiro, I would just give it a pass. There are plenty of options out there when it comes to Souls-like games, so I am not too worried.
Hell, even the new Lords of the Fallen was more enjoyable to me than this game was, and I had more fun in the 30-minutes I spent playing the Onimusha Demo, then I had in the entirety of my time with Elden Ring (though, granted, Onimusha isn't really a souls-like).

comment:
I only have a few things against this game but I think it's enough to say don't buy it for this current price get it on sale

1. The combat is actually good just not for me this is my first real turn based strategy game and I can say I don't like it if you haven't played a TBSG or do like it ignore this point I think it's worth giving a shot if you haven't already

2. I have a decent PC not the best but decent the amount of visual bugs glitches and performance issues I got from act 3 is insane I would not recommend this game for those with potato pcs since act 3 takes up like 60% of your gameplay

3. the time it takes to complete a playthrough is insane you see my hours on this game? that's from 2 playthroughs and what's worse for all this time the pacing is horrible act 1 is simply too long for it's on good act 2 is decent no complaints there but somehow act 3 is rushed I can't explain it well but It's big quest after big quest with no room to sit around and just contemplate your next move if you wanna finish this game quickly bc trust me when you get to act 3 you want to finish this game quickly

4. the writing of the characters if actually good i like their personalities but when it comes to plot their goals ect its trash there's so many times characters just betray you for no reason when you look at their original personality just to make the endgame harder not to mention the character contradictions that are never mentioned like karlach using soul coins which is a BIG no no in DND lore when she's meant to be the nice one of the group or astarion after killing cazador not drinking his blood and becoming a true vampire

5. speaking of endgame it sucks the boss fight is anti climatic you just distract a dragon enter a portal and kill a brain that can't fight back Rapheal despite being optional is 100% the better boss fight

6. due to the mediocre main quest and act 3 fatigue I just don't wanna replay it anymore despite all the characters and roles I could choose like I wanna try to be a bard or a rouge but why would i drop another 40 hours of my life on a game I already completed? I'd only do that if the game was REALLY good and this game Isn't that

7. on a more trivial note the romance SUCKS the pacing is either too fast for the relationship or the relationship doesn't exist speaking of which you might as well be playing a solo game with no companions with how little interaction you have with them and how little they speak about the environment yk it's bad when Fo4 has you beat on that

8. like most rpgs your choices do not matter there's practically 3 main endings and that's it you can kill spare or torture as many people as you want doesn't matter except maybe a tonal shift between companions there's no ending slides like FNV


not to say this game is all bad I love the origin characters personalities (not tav or durge they feel blank as if they don't exist even durge could be replaced with any other character and it wouldn't make a difference) I like the side quests and I love the boss fights outside of the brain oh and I LOVE LOVE the soundtrack but at the current state I wish I did not buy BG3 I regret it and I hate how it took me till act 2 to realize how boring this game was that's sad the game isn't inherently bad it's just boring and I think that's worse imo

6/10 game definition of an okay game I don't understand the hype if you want an rpg with amazing replayability good characters play skyrim FNV anything from the early 2010s modern rpgs just suck tbh

comment:
The game's resurrection from its first release through Phantom Liberty is well documented. A bug filled failure, victim of greed and crunches. But instead of walking away with their tail firmly between their legs, CDPR took the complaints and criticisms to heart, and began a long-term renovation. By patch 1.61, the game actually was playable and you didn't wait for the inevitable crash. With patch 2.0, they rewrote everything from skill trees to fundamental game play. Phantom Liberty may be the only DLC released for the game, but it's one of the best, period. 

The game is based on Mike Pondsmith's TTRPG, and the influence of that game is all over the DNA of 2077. CDPR made changes to fit a video game better, but the fundamental story of living in a world under corporate oppression, the wealthy beyond the law's reach, and survival meaning sometimes giving up on your dreams, remains. The graphics, five years later, are still a benchmark. The story and the characters will draw you in, and your choices often make more of a difference than you think. 

If you can't tell, I love this game. 1300+ hours (and counting), I still find new things every playthrough.

comment:
Title: Never Fade Away...

A lot of time has passed since launch, and only now can I truly say it: this game is a masterpiece. The work CD Projekt Red put into turning this around is fantastic.

The plot tackles real, massive issues reflecting our own world. This isn't just a brief main quest that feels like a small add-on to a massive map—it’s a deeply human story filled with heroes, villains, and losers. It asks what it really takes for a "nobody" to become a legend, and more importantly, what price you pay for that success. This is pure, authentic Cyberpunk. To be honest, I wasn't sure CDPR could pull it off, but the voice acting and performances are fabulous. They brought Night City to life so convincingly that you instantly buy into its ruthless rules and struggles.

Gameplay at launch was okay, but weak. Today? It’s phenomenal. The world is packed with hidden details, easter eggs, and its own urban legends. As for bugs, I rarely ran into anything major—just the occasional floating car or clipping geometry. For where the game stands today, it plays great. It just needs a few tiny polish tweaks, but nothing that ruins the experience.

The map is huge, and the DLC filled in every empty space seamlessly. There are countless small stories to uncover and interesting places to explore. The level design and world-building deserve serious praise.

Summary:
Without spoiling anything: trust me, you won't regret playing this. It’s far from a typical video game story—it’s something much deeper. Accept the rules of Night City, jump in, and experience it. The writing and acting ensure this world never feels like a hollow cardboard set; the city is cruel, and you will feel every bit of it.

Score: 9/10 (Play it, and you’ll understand why).

comment:
If you love playing DnD for an equal mix of roleplay and optimizing for combat, and you have a decent idea of how DnD works you'll be set to know what you're doing in building a character and playing in turn based combat. If not, there is a learning curve at the top of the game, you're going to have a lot of options thrown at you and it's a lot to learn all at once. On the other hand as well if you are expecting an exact 1:1 replica of 5e tabletop play, you'll probably be grumpy too, but if you can accept that they had to jigsaw 5e rules to work in a video game because they can't possibly account for every single subclass, spell, or feat the way you can on table top then you'll learn to love the off center replica of DnD.
All of the romances have different weights, but you don't HAVE to romance any of the characters if you don't want. Your decisions do actually effect the way your companions view you as well, so not everyone will take an interest in your character, some may be antagonistic towards you, but it is possible to keep everyone pleasant with you without too much going out of your way. That being said there is also lots of replay ability, you can zig zag all over the place with choices, explore different paths, go wild with it. If you're set on one specific way of things going, you're going to have to save scum a lot, but it's not impossible to get your ideal outcome.
Of course the voice acting is amazing, the writing is excellent and varied, the locations are stunning, the story arc is great, so on so forth.

My only complaint is the multiplayer is a little janky. Ran into so many glitches playing with friends that I never have in my solo runs. Save often if you play with friends over distance so you can reload as needed.

Other than that, I love the game top to bottom, I will still be playing this decades from now I am sure.

comment:
I went into this open-minded, and with no spoilers. Big mistake. 14 hours into the game, I feel like I would have had more fun watching someone else on their second playthrough, rather than experiencing it myself for the first time.

Great writing and characters, but it's not a fun game.

The game wants you to explore the world and characters, but actually railroads you. Step 2 feet off the invisible "intended" path because the game suggests that you should? Have fun reloading after getting melted by a single frog or whatever + being forced to reload your save.

The good:
- The decisions you make, and the story itself is very malleable and impressively adaptive. 
- The characters are interesting. 
- The story is fun and engaging.

The bad:
- It's actually railroaded, despite how adaptive and free it may appear. You must follow exactly whatever the developers intended, in some way or another, and the illusion of choice is frustrating. 
- If you don't know how to deal with an encounter, you're screwed. The game doesn't teach you how to play, what's dangerous, or what's important. Have fun reloading your saves multiple times because you didn't know that a fight was coming, or realising that an enemy being 1 level above you stops you from progressing AT ALL, and then being forced to go and do something else. Combat is absolutely trial and error.

The ugly:
- Inventory management is not fun.
- Unless you've played DND before, you're basically guessing what everything does. 
- Tutorial pop-ups are sparse.

comment:
The lack of a third person mode really hurts the roleplay of the story, its hard to get in character when V is such a blank slate that you dont even know who you should be roleplaying as, and she isnt such a blank slate that you can print a character you want to play as, so getting fully into character as one would in RDR2 or GTA5 is nigh impossible.

The gameplay is janky, buggy, and messy. Certain time slowing effects like "slow time on reload" or "slow time when health is low" do not add much while (in the case of slow time on reload) actively drag out gameplay. (these are optional of course but it just feels bad because what are you supposed to do while reloading? alt tab and find a youtube video to watch while the reload animation just takes twice as long?)

You're likely to go about 10 minutes into the game before encountering a game breaking glitch that either makes you reload a save or waste your time trying to figure out what's going on. in my playthrough, i encountered a weapon drop off point (for those quests that force you to put your weapons away before entering a club) that ate my weapons and didnt let me retrieve them, forcing a reload; A sniper that was glitched into the floor that I could not take out stealth and was forced to kill via quickhacks, which then sucked him back into the room, aggro'd of course; Adam Smasher clipped into a wall and ate bullets for 5 minutes before getting flinched backwards enough to clip himself back inbounds, taking a solid half his health out before i was able to actually continue the fight. yeah yeah just reload, but that sucks! you shouldn't have to do that!

the world feels empty, there are no real consequences for going on mass killing sprees despite cyberpsychosis being a major plot point in the world of cyberpunk, and the characters feel lifeless and uninteresting, making it somehow even harder to get into the roleplay aspect of this ROLEPLAYING GAME

Also, only being able to respec one time per playthrough is SO BAD, genuinely its just a singleplayer game WHY is this a thing? and not being able to customize weapons after a mod is put in it? thats just being ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ for the sake of being a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ game. god forbid a player wants to mix things up instead of hard committing to a single build in a SINGLE PLAYER GAME.

overall, 6/10. just play RDR2 and have a much better time.

🎮 The Witcher 3 Next-Gen: Ultra Path Tracing Guide for Mid-Range Specs (RTX 5060 Ti 16GB / i5-12400)
If you want to experience The Witcher 3 Remastered with full Path Tracing on mid-range hardware without the game turning into a slideshow, this setup balances maximum visual fidelity, smooth performance, and image sharpness.
By leveraging the massive 16GB VRAM pool on this specific GPU and using Reshade to counter upscaling blur, you can get a locked, beautiful 60 FPS experience on a 4K TV.
🖥️ Hardware Setup
• GPU: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060 Ti 16GB (Note: The 16GB VRAM is mandatory here. The 8GB version will completely collapse under these path-tracing settings).
• CPU: Intel Core i5-12400
• Display: 4K TV (60Hz / HDR) running at an actual 1440p pixel ratio
⚙️ In-Game Settings
• Graphics Preset: Ultra
• Ray Tracing: ON (Path Tracing Enabled)
• DLSS: Performance Mode
• DLSS Frame Generation: ON
• NVIDIA Reflex: ON + Boost (Highly recommended to mitigate Frame Gen latency)
🎨 Visual Enhancement (The Secret Sauce)
• Reshade: Enabled (Using sharpening filters like CAS or LumaSharpen).
• Why? This completely counteracts the softness introduced by DLSS Performance mode, giving you the crispness of a native resolution without the massive performance hit.
📊 Performance & Metric Results
• Frame Rate: Locked 60 FPS (matching the TV's refresh rate).
• GPU Usage: ~75% Utilization. Because Frame Generation easily pushes the game to the TV's 60Hz limit, the GPU doesn't need to max out at 100%. This keeps the card running cooler and quieter.
• CPU Usage: ~45% to 50% Utilization. The i5-12400 has plenty of breathing room, completely eliminating any processor bottlenecks.
• Input Latency / Feel: Played with an Xbox Controller. While Frame Generation introduces a slight input delay, playing on a controller naturally smooths out camera movements, making the latency completely unnoticeable during actual gameplay.
(If you turn Frame Gen OFF, native performance sits around 45 FPS in most places and dips to 35 FPS in dense, shadowy areas or Novigrad. Using Frame Generation is heavily recommended to smooth out those drops).

comment:
Elden Ring is easily one of my favorite games ever. The world actually feels like a world. I still remember wandering into Caelid way too early and getting humbled. That kind of thing happens all the time: you spot something weird in the distance, ride over, and end up in some dungeon fighting a boss you weren't ready for. That loop never got old for me.

Combat is brutal but fair. When you die, it's usually because you messed up, not because the game cheated. The build variety is insane. I've done strength, faith, and bleed builds, and they all feel viable. Boss fights are the highlight. Some are absolutely infuriating, but beating them is one of the best feelings in gaming.

Yeah, it has issues. The camera can be awful in big fights, and some quests are so vague you'll need a guide. But the good far outweighs the bad. If you want a game that respects your intelligence and rewards curiosity, play it. Just be ready to die a lot.

comment:
After Dark Souls III introduced me to the Souls formula, Elden Ring felt like the natural next step and apparently all those hours spent learning to "git gud" actually paid off.

I had very similar feelings about Elden Ring to the ones I had about DS3, although this time around I found the experience somewhat easier. Not because the game doesn't have its fair share of difficult bosses and encounters, but because I already knew what these games expected from me. DS3 had taught me to be patient, learn attack patterns, adapt and try again rather than immediately panic when something wanted to murder me.

And yes, I'm still a magic user. Some things never change. 😅

The move to an open world worked beautifully for me. There's an enormous amount to explore, and discovering completely new areas while simply wandering around the Lands Between was one of my favourite parts of the experience.

The Eternal Cities were easily my favourite locations. Nokron and Nokstella have such a beautiful, otherworldly atmosphere that discovering them for the first time really stuck with me.

My favourite boss, though, has to be Rennala, Queen of the Full Moon. Maybe there's a slight magical bias there... 🌙

I enjoyed the story and lore as well. Like Dark Souls, Elden Ring gives you a world where there's always more beneath the surface if you're willing to look for it, and piecing everything together is part of the experience.

The soundtrack is fantastic too, especially some of the boss themes and, as seems to be becoming a tradition with games I love, several tracks inevitably ended up on my Spotify playlists.

Shadow of the Erdtree was also a great addition and gave me another reason to return to a world I'd already spent so much time exploring.

Dark Souls III taught me how to "git gud". Elden Ring gave me an enormous world in which to put that lesson to use.

And, naturally, I did most of it by throwing magic at things from a safe distance. 🧙‍♂️✨

comment:
Counter-Strike 2: A Song of Smoke and Betrayal
Hear ye, hear ye, Lords and Ladies of the Competitive Realm!

Counter-Strike 2 is a battlefield worthy of legends. A game of steel nerves, cunning strategies, and glorious headshots. Here, friendships are forged in fire, rivalries are born in blood, and every round is a tale worthy of the bards. The thrill of clutching a 1v5 is sweeter than victory at the Iron Throne, and the sound of an AWP firing is music to the ears of even the coldest lord of Westeros.

The skins? Oh, what a splendid treasury! From crimson blades worthy of House Lannister to dragon-lore rifles fit for the Targaryens, one may adorn their arsenal in magnificent fashion. For in this realm, it is not merely how you slay your foes, but how gloriously you do so.

The competition is fierce, the stakes are high, and when both teams are evenly matched, the battles are glorious. Every smoke is a scheme, every flash a deception, and every defuse a race against the Stranger himself.

BUT LO, A DARKNESS GATHERS BEYOND THE WALL.

For this realm is plagued by a most vile affliction: the poison of cheaters.

Wallhackers, who see through stone as if blessed by the Three-Eyed Raven. Aimbotters, whose arrows never miss, whose bullets find skulls with the certainty of a prophecy. Suspicious lords who turn corners with knowledge no mortal ought to possess. They roam the servers like White Walkers, corrupting the living and extinguishing the joy of honest warriors.

And what of the honourable player who trains for countless hours, perfects their aim, studies the maps, and fights with all the skill they possess? They are left wondering whether they were bested by a better warrior or struck down by some foul sorcery beyond the laws of the realm.

'Tis a cruel fate, to enter the arena seeking glory, only to discover that the enemy has brought a dragon to a knife fight.

Still, when the stars align, the teams are fair, and the cheaters are banished beyond the Wall, Counter-Strike 2 remains a magnificent contest of skill, teamwork, and nerve.

My verdict, therefore, is this:

A glorious game with the heart of a champion, the soul of a warrior, and the potential to rule the Seven Kingdoms of competitive shooters.

Yet its throne is besmirched by treachery, and its kingdom weakened by those who forsake honour for hollow victories.

Valve, the realm cries out for justice! Sharpen thy anti-cheat, strengthen the Watch, and cast these foul sorcerers into the frozen wastes!

For a kingdom cannot thrive when its honest warriors grow weary of fighting shadows.

Would I recommend it? Aye.

But I would sooner trust a Lannister with my gold than trust every death replay in this cursed realm.

Winter is coming. And apparently, so is another spinbotter.

comment:
Disclaimer: This is a Remaster review. The Witcher 3 I played back on PS4 is still a masterpiece. 

As someone who has put over 1600 mods into Skyrim, this feels like a heavily modded version of TW3, not a true remaster. I know they already did a next-gen update, so they had to call this something different, but calling it a remaster was a mistake. It does not live up to the expectations that word sets.

This remaster has stripped away a lot of the magic by desaturating the color and making everything look more realistic. The original game looks like a beautiful painting. This game looks like an unreal tech demo where they think higher quality bushes and realistic lighting constitutes better art direction. It doesn't.

The lighting changes/additions are not well executed at all. Putting aside the complete loss of the original's brilliant color grading and art direction, ray tracing and path tracing look decent outdoors. However indoors is a different story. Ray tracing sometimes works indoors, but path tracing almost never works indoors. Half the huts in White Orchard are pitch black indoors, including ones with quest NPCs. I had to keep switching between PT and RT and raster to try and get the least bad lighting for the moment. Not best lighting, least bad. 

Menus are weirdly laggy and glitchy, and somehow the fps seems lower in them even those steam tells me I'm getting 100+ frames. Again, how did that get missed? 

Geralt attacks non-existent enemies instead of the one right in front of him. I'm sure that was a problem in the original game, but for a remaster that supposedly fixing the combat issues...they are still there, unfixed. 

After nearly completing White Orchard, I think I'm just going to roll back and play the original version of the game, or maybe the next-gen. From what I've researched it's generally more faithful to the original vision.

comment:
A beautiful, open-world Souls Like that most will probably enjoy, especially if they are new to the genre. Technically it's the entry with the most new gameplay mechanics and stunning graphics as well as amount of bosses and areas to explore/clear out, however, aside from that it doesn't have much else better from previous titles.

I played through DS2 and all the DLCs as well as NG+, it's my only experience with the series but it was a really good one. So when I entered the world of Elden Ring I had similar expectations of the bosses and enemies and general ideea of exploration, except they couldn't be applied. ER takes such a inbetween position of gameplay that it utterly annoys me how disrespectful it is to the player, it tries to stay on two stools, one which is Dark Soul's movement/dodge based wait out with punishment to the boss after their combo, and to the Sekiro's/Bloodborne aggressiveness of the enemies/the player...? 

Most notably the only real mobility change the player gets in combat is jumping, which would have been a nice addition if it wasn't for how ridiculously inertialess it feels. Finding the actual gap where you can attack the enemies and bosses freely or at least even just trade with them - is extremely tiring. The recovery time for the combo's are so short your gameplay will be 95% of the time just seeing someone's body and a bunch of metal sounds and bright flashes while constantly spamming dodge. Dark Souls at least had you use your actual positioning/walking/running and not just dodge rolling at the correct time so you had  a more balanced type of gameplay between the boss and yourself.

Horseback fighting is also extremely clunky and unsatisfying, most enemies that were designed around it are really not entertaining to fight against because they are so much easier when using the horse. It should have stayed as a mode of transportation since the springstream mechanic is quite fun and the world is already pretty big. To continue - the world being big doesnt necessarily mean it's shallow as a puddle, but I would have definetely preffered if they condensed the world by 2x and not made the curious player feel like they waste time 90% of the time. Dark Souls while linear would always reward curious players, so when i came over to ER and started looking over each nook and cranny only to get useless crafting materials - well it's just discouraging and feels like the developer trying to take out as much time out of you as possible.

Ashes of War are perhaps the only good mechanic that came out of this entry and even then from the little use that I did have with them, it seems most are extremely niche and likely to never be used in favor of other objectively better ones leaving 90% of them to never be used and be clutter. Take this with a grain of salt as I didn't use them all that much.

Overall, while the game is good and many new players will enjoy it - I wouldn't buy it if you are self respecting Dark Souls fan. The game caters rather hardly to the hardcore players and I say this as a DS2 fan which had the same allegations thrown against it. Elden Ring is through and through made to break your patience and test just how much are you ready to adapt to it's bosses and new mechanics constantly. God forbid you are a UGS user in this game, good-♥♥♥♥♥♥♥-luck, you will need it.

comment:
Elden Ring is probably the worst FromSoft / Souls game I have played. Its not a *bad* game by any means but compared to the other main line Souls / FromSoft games it is. 

Before getting into what I don't like about this game, I will say a few positive things. The game looks beautiful and runs pretty well all things considered. The voice acting, characters, verity of enemies, locations, etc... are also all well done, and even though I don't like open world games because they are usually slop filled with nothing, Elden Ring somehow manages to make it feel more alive and actually have things to discover and do. Thats about all the compliments I can give it though. 

For the things I don't like, for starters, its a painfully easy game. I have no idea how people are saying its the hardest souls like game or harder than Sekiro, both I hear quite a bit in the spaces I am in online or the videos I watch. Granted I have not yet finished the game yet, I cannot bring myself to do so, it feels like im forcing myself to play this game. But I still do have (I think) enough playtime to form some sort of opinion based on what I have played. From the bosses and enemies I have had to fight, none of them were difficult, and most only took 1-2 tries. I know there are probably harder enemies and bosses in the rest of the base game, and DLC (from what ive heard) but thats not the main problem I have with this game. I do plan on eventually completing the game and DLC, but until I do that my review will stay as is and I doubt it will change. 

The main issue I have with this game is that for most of my time playing its straight up riding on horseback going from one castle or cave to the next while having to fight pathetically easy ass enemies in between. At first it was really cool riding a horse and exploring the world, but eventually it got boring and tedious. I know one of my compliments was that there were things to discover and explore, and that is true, once you found a new castle or cave or whatever to get into THAT was fun, but for the other majority of the game, you are just left riding on a horse until you get to those fun parts, and even then they don't last very long sadly. Maybe I just prefer the more "linear" (I don't think Dark Souls 1 is linear) Dark Souls games, but for most of the time, it never felt dull, repetitive, or felt like I was simply waiting for there to be a fun moment like I do with this game. I get its an open world game, but its still. The reason I don't have this issue with RDR or RDR2 is because the combat while on your horse in those games is actually fun, and there's more you can do with your companion, even having a bonding level with the horse and various other mechanics. I think they dropped the ball not making the 1 animal your around for 99% of the game have more mechanics than just feeding them when they have low HP. 

Another thing is that at least for me there was almost nothing rememberable about this game compared to the other ones. I can think of several moments, enemies, characters, etc... from the other souls games, sekiro, bloodborne, that have stuck with me off the top of my head. The only cool thing I can remember is when you are about to fight Radahn you can see other characters in the game at the Castle ready to be summoned and fight alongside you. As far as im aware its the first time you could summon this many people and it felt very cinematic and cool. Again, something really cool that happens because its a main boss / castle. Another L for the rest of the open world area. I just find it extremely funny that even though its an open world game, the best parts is when you aren't in the open world, like in a castle, cave, etc... 

I think this game would have benefited from being not open world, or at the very least having a smaller world. Again, I do plan to finish this game eventually, and change my review accordingly, but until then all I can say is that as a game itself it is fun somewhat, but compared to the other Souls games or From Soft games, its the weakest one. 

I do expect alot of criticism / hate and I suppose theres nothing I can do about that, but these are just my opinions and if you enjoyed the game I'm happy that you did. 

7/10 (review will change eventually).

comment:
Highly Rated, But a Tedious and Punishing Trial-and-Error Experience
Rating: Not Recommended
If you are buying this game based on its glowing masterwork reviews, hoping for a smooth and immersive fantasy RPG adventure to relax with after work, you should think twice.
1. Extremely Vague and Frustrating Mission Guidance
The quest design offers little to no clear directional guidance. Instead of rewarding exploration, the system leaves you to blindly fumble around huge maps. This lack of structure leads to aimless wandering rather than any real sense of discovery.
2. Punishing Invisible Traps and Chain-Aggro Mechanics
What is often praised as "unrivaled freedom" is actually a hyper-fussy physical and rule simulator. Simply walking over to inspect an area can trigger beast aggression, call over guards, and sound alarm drums—instantly turning an entire encampment hostile and forcing a GAME OVER. A single misstep can wipe out tens of minutes or hours of progress, creating immense frustration.
3. Tedious Micro-Management and Fractured Combat
The combination of mandatory turn-based combat and complex D&D rules makes every action feel like solving a math problem. Party members frequently unlink or get stuck behind terrain, requiring constant, tedious micromanagement. The combat lacks fluid feedback and feels more like administrative homework than rewarding gameplay.
Summary:
This game may appeal to hardcore players who have endless free time to study tabletop rulebooks and enjoy trial-and-error reloading. However, for players seeking a fluid, enjoyable fantasy adventure with direct positive feedback, playing this is simply an exercise in frustration.

comment:
I've put off buying this game since release. The reason: the original teaser showed a very gritty very brutal and harsh world. The first gameplay trailer showed it to be "GTA but reskinned to future tech".

But due to a deep sale I gave it a shot.

It's alright. It's definitely entertaining. But it's not the game I was hoping it would be. It's not the "Blade Runner" dark dystopian vibes. It's more "GTA meets Saints Row" vibes. "haha d*ck implants malfunction" vibes. The characters are all caricatures, stereotypes, blown to the extremes. Voice lines sometimes feel like they recorded them out of order over several sessions with no cohesion or flow. You are constantly being slammed by messages and calls and side information but there really isn't that much reason to read it all because there's very little substance to the world building and it feels tedious. It also doesn't feel like you actually change the course of the game at all as often your dialog options are the same but just worded differently. 

If we look at gameplay: the main missions offer a bunch of ways to get the objective done. That's cool. Outside of that there's no dialog options to talk your way out of things. Stealth is not really rewarded and a lot of it is just combat. The combat in itself is pretty alright but at higher difficulty enemies just become spongy and your weapons generally feel quite weak making a human take as many bullets to the head as a full on robot. For a Saints Row game that's what I'd expect. I was hoping for something a little better here.

Overall with the expectation of an immersive dystopian RPG I can't give it more than a 6/10. It's fun. It works well as 'mindless entertainment' (although admittedly there's to much in the sense of unskipable cutscenes / dialog in the game to be purely that.... just the 'intro' to the game took me 4 hours while not doing that much besides getting to the title screen. Dialog where you don't really have options aside from saying the same thing 2 different ways which in the end doesn't matter).

I think the framework for this game is solid. The art direction is very cool. The music is solid. The factions and stuff that's all good. If they every make a part 2 I hope they invest more into it being an actual RPG more akin to Deus Ex or Mass Effect (although... well controversial ending... but that aside) and that they make it a bit more grounded and gritty.

comment:
Writing this is say that on release the Remaster visually feels like a downgrade from Next Gen.

The lighting in the game I think focuses on realism over visual aesthetic and clarity: contrast in the game is muted, certain areas like the castle in skellige turned grey and muddy in comparisons next gen's warm lights and cool shadows. Holding up a torch washes out Geralt into a dusty yellow with even lower contrast.... the bloom and harsh lighting and details hidden due to distance or shadows has been removed. Sometimes shadows obscuring things is good! Lets you focus on the characters and creates beleivable depth.

Upon opening the game, the sensitivity that I had in Next-Gen became dizzyinng in the Remaster. This might be due to the fact Geralt is now smaller and closer to the center of the screen. In my opinion, the closer "over the shoulder"-like camera felt more immersive and was easier to see with, but that absolutely is a to each their own thing.

Finally, I was super excited for all the new features added to camera-mode, but the scroll to zoom-in doesnt work for now, and I find the mouse working on the camera more disorienting than anything. While you can add characteers and props, I didnt see an option to moving around characters on XYZ to fit into where I pointed the camera. Its probably just a learning curb, but with the whole lighting, contrast and color grading situation, I'd rather downgrade back to next-gen to take photos and run around in the game.

I dont have much to say about gameplay, I didn't get far enough into the remaster to play as the stuff I stated above was enough to have me back out. Hopefully the upcoming DLC will be Next Gen friendly but I doubt it..

I enjoy playing the Witcher 3, but ATM I cant reccomend the Remaster in terms of visuals ( and my fan getting louder ) ... Theres probably things I can do to adjust controls, but nothings going to change that color grading fn so yeah.

comment:
If you're looking for a bit of shallow fun, go for it. It's essentially a hybrid of Farcry games and a GTA style open world with a sci-fi noir theme. Turn your brain off and follow the quest marker while enjoying a power fantasy. If you were hoping for more immersive sim elements, It doesn't get any deeper than that unfortunately. 

Something about the story/writing is a bit too edgy for me so that hasn't drawn me in. The graphics are nice but Night City is 99% set dressing with a bunch of meaninless filler slaped around. On normal dificulty,  you're essentially a god from the get-go and can run and gun your way out of most situations. The RPG mechanics are pretty surface level too. Don't expect a well crafted progressoin curve. Most perks and chrome are just a few percentage points, though you can unlock things like double jump etc. though it still feels a bit empty to me. 

The gameplay loops is going from mission to mission. Don't expect an intriocate world like Skyrim. While there are a few forks in the quests, it's nothing like what you might find in Obsidian titles. Most of the decisions you make are pretty unimportant.

comment:
First of all: dialogues are awesome, so are the characters. But this just ain't for me.

- weird timed restrictions (started new game 3 times, never was able to get Karlachs romance to work despite using guides)
- fights get really frustrating, when you keep missing at 90% while enemies always land attacks
- rng in general, with events -> ends in try, load, repeat

+ amazing characters and dialogues
+ runs extremely well while looking great
+ deep rpg systems (loads of optimization etc.)
+ unique and great quests
+ story could get interesting (never finished act 1 because of the negatives above)

Overall I love choices in games, to an extend. Here however it just got more stressful and annoying then anything else. Always fearing I miss something (I don't have the time for several playthroughs) combined with easily missable events because you didn't sleep two times in a row and such. And then the RNG, which results in save, try, repeat... And the game just wouldn't let me get a good playthrough, even while using guides. So I quit.

comment:
The game have awful technical issues on Windows 11 PC:
- it claims that it runs in 60 fps while it refreshes display randomly, so the display has 100hz while game claims to be 60fps which makes everything clunky and not smooth
- randomly chaning windows settings can make input delay significantly longer e.g switching on HDR makes game more responsive because input is processed 30ms faster for no reason
- immune frames do not apply instantly after releasing roll button as in any other souls game. Because game was natively developed for 30fps control there is an issue that 3 first frames are not immune
- fullscreen mode prove excruciating 100ms of delay!!! only playing in borderless mode is possible
- no support for nvidia reflex
- GSYNC apparently provide 30ms od delay
- after switching off game display flickers randomly (it happpens only with this game)
-  there are many settings in NVIDIA control panel that further change input delay like VSYNC (which is not to be set in game but switching it off or setting to fast changes a lot)
- turning off some setting in WINDOWS 11 that usually make game run better make input delay longer for 10 - 30 ms. e.g Variable Refresh Rate
All of these I recorded while playing and calculated average delay. I played a bit of DS3 to check if there is such an issue but no. In DS3 response to the action is so quick that feels weird and even too quick after playing Elden Ring. I cannot recommend this game even though i spend a lot time with it but half of it was fighting technical issue and reading about so called "Dentalion" Game Engine that FromSoftware uses. All of the problem are documented or easily documented using developer tools. But you know there are people who will always say "Git gut" and start yapping about button working on release, So the problem will never get a proper patch.

Without touching the online multiplayer, the base single-player campaign on its own feels incredibly overrated, tedious, and dates itself pretty hard. The open world might be massive, but the actual mission design feels rigid and restricted unless you are using mods to completely tear the game apart and play it your own way.

comment:
I'm sure this game is very successful at what it sets out to do, but I bounced off it hard. It's supposedly an RPG, but you can really only play two types of character: Hack a Bunch of Stuff and Also Shoot a Bunch of People, or Shoot Everyone. There really doesn't seem to be any other approach you can take. My first character was a street kid, and I made him Black, inspired by one of the hairstyles. But there's only one male voice, and it's a dirtbag white voice, and it didn't fit the character at all. So I immediately restarted and created a female corporate character. The voice fit, but the prologue quest suggested a double-cross choice that I wanted to take but wasn't permitted to, after which the game thrusts the player into a bleak introductory mission that's pretty much entirely on rails. A training sequence suggests that nonlethal takedowns are a thing, but then the game basically tells you that they're a bad idea and that you should just kill everybody. I was hoping for Neuromancer, but it felt more like Grand Theft Auto.

Also, despite the fact that my character was supposed to have superb reflexes, I couldn't make the dodge controls work. I'm a piano player; if I can't press the right keys at the right time, that is not a well-designed key sequence. In short, it was shaping up to be a grim, frustrating experience that didn't allow me the kinds of choices I wanted to make and had been taught by other games to expect that I could make, so I bailed out and requested a refund. I guess I'll never learn whether or not it deserves the hype, because I wasn't excited by anything that happened in my first two hours of play.

Don't throw me into a dystopia and then not let me fight the Man.

comment: Game is honestly very bad and I don't get the hype around it at all. Full of bugs, balance on higher difficulty is horrible, most perks you unlock or cyberwear don't give any meaningful bonuses, fist figthing is so bad it's unbelievable (enemies attack air a couple meters away from you and you still take damage, parrying is supposed to negate damage but you still take damage). In the beginning, the game takes your car away from you for absolutely no reason so you can't drive, but instead you just get 30 fast travel points everywhere around town so there's no point in driving anyways because you can just teleport everywhere. You also immediately get a million markers on the map so it's another brain-dead game: go to markers, do some quick boring thing to complete it, rinse and repeat. You are CONSTANTLY being called on your phone by some random NPCs you've never met who act like they know you and call you to tell you they have a job for you. It happens ALL THE TIME even in the middle of other quests and conversations with characters so you get double dialogue at the same time (YOU CAN"T REJECT THE PHONE CALLS, your character answers automatically, even though the game says there's a reject button) and it interrupts your dialogue during missions and breaks all the immersion and flow of mission and conversations. The game doesn't know how to handle it because you are in 2 dialogues at the same time that are playing and you are in situations where you have to pick a dialogue option to answer for 2 dialogues at the same time (which the game doesn't handle at all and it bugs out, especially if you get the "timed" response situation where you have to quickly pick a reponse in dialogue and the time runs out but the game doesn't let you pick the response because someone called you and intercepted the dialogue so it ruins your other conversation). And I can't stress it enough, it happens ALL THE TIME (it's happened like 10+ times during ~10 hours of gameplay (I have 20 hours, but first 10 is the intro before you get to the actual game and it starts happening)). The city also honestly feels dead, there's nothing interesting going on, for a game where the city was a big selling point I thought, there's really nothing to do, nothing and no-one you can interact with (other than the specified markers on the map with the "mini quests"). You won't run into any interesting situations, you can't just walk around and enter some clubs or something, there's a ton of buildings and clubs etc everywhere and you can't enter anywhere, they're just facades. NPCs just spawn and despawn randomly if you turn around even next to you and sometimes even right in front of your eyes. The only good thing about this game honestly are the voice acting and dialogues (especially in main missions) but even these very quickly get boring because it feels like 90% of the game is listening to dialogues and only 10% is actual gameplay. There's a stealth system and you should be able to sneak up to enemies from behind to perform takedowns but 50% of the time the prompt for that just doesn't show up and you just stand there crounching behing an enemy like an idiot for 20 seconds and can't do anything until someone spots you.  When you enter a vehicle, the game often just stars playing some random radio station and it continues to play after you leave the vehicle. You have to open a radio menu and scroll through a whole list of radio stations to the "No station" option and select it to disable the music. EVERY TIME. I did a side quest where you have an optional objective to find out some secret information that is needed to prevent an NPC from killing himself. I did it and the guy still killed himself because apparently you have to pick a specific dialogue option later (neither dialogue option suggests what's gonna happen and the one that prevents him from killing himself is clearly the wrong one if you did the optional quest but I guess the devs didn't talk to each other so yea, let's ♥♥♥♥ up the players playthrough). Sometimes your character just randomly climbs something in from of them even if you don't press the jump/climb button. I've had it happen when doing a mission stealthily and my character would just expose themself by climbing a cover I was hinding behind. One time I was covering behind a fence during a shootout and my character just climbed it and jumped down behind it, several stories down and I just died. I seriously can keep going on with this crap for hours and I literally just started the game. On top of that, the game still crashes occasionally (after several years?) and whenever you launch the game you have to watch an insanely long unskippable intro of logos you don't care about and other crap and people have to make mods to let you skip it. What a game! I put off buying this game for years and I finally bought it and I honestly regret it, not worth it at all.

comment:
If I could give a mixed recommendation, I would, including for Liberty City.
Summary for folks who want the brief - the main game plot is supposed to be a ticking time bomb where the MC have a limited time to save themselves, despite the worldbuilding and the core gameplay design contradicting it.
That's it, now for a more critical reflection below.

Unlike previous Witcher projects, the main storyline is relatively quick (20-30 hours). For people who defends the game with all the side quests and Phantom Liberty DLC, the gameplay doesn't reflect the ticking time bomb. There is no timer for quests, and since you are somewhat expected to reach multiple endings by playing through branching side quests, you actually lose the plot and momentum by doing everything else.

Imagine if you play Red Dead 2, but on the last arc - you feel like something is missing if you didn't experience the freedom and glorious adventures in the previous arcs. CPK have this issue, and it's terribly rushed with some characters' arc being noticably trimmed down. You either have to forgo the mentality of a ticking time bomb, or you get the worst and more unrewarding main story content if you choose to focus on it.

I play main as female V because she, like Kassandra from AC: Odyssey, have the better VA. V's background honestly feels underwhelming and only affects some of the choices you will make, like getting more money. For a corpo, she doesn't feel like it, and the decision to age her down from 28 to 23 does affect your believability of her. 
The game also over-balanced itself after patch 1.6, removing many fun previous mechanics like shooting through walls, hacking through walls, putting silencers on other guns besides pistols, and more customizability. Now, it kinda forces you to balance your character and build, which isn't as fun.

Everything else besides the main plot, including the characters, world, and combat, are all very fun. It is basically the Witcher gameplay with sci-fi elements. You can feel the project is rushed before the scope of their destination is reached, and I love the world so much I feel like it ruins part of the experience for me.
Hell, I'd argue the overbalanced nature of later patches was because the overall game, including sidequests, are maybe 80-100 hours in total content and it isn't nearly enough to have a bigger and more complex skill tree.

I also gave it a bad review because, like many cultured players, the decision to not add romance for both Aurore and So Mi cripples me for days and I had to install mods to regain small parts of my sanity. Despite this game promising a lot, the romance and a few quests felt short of, well, being short. There is something amazing here if they choose to tap into more, and I hope their Orion project sequel will deliver.

comment:
The remaster, while it does make the game look much more impressive than before SOMETIMES, is actually not worth your time. Why only sometimes? Because the remaster also introduces a metric crapton of visual glitches that weren't there before. Flickering textures, overbright lighting, you name it, it's got it.

The new graphic settings menu is also extremely buggy on controller. Some settings not "letting go" of your cursor, randomly popping out of the menu and back into the main menu, ...

Some settings also don't do what they say they do. For instance, changing the preset on DLSS to any other setting does absolutely nothing. Turning DLSS off altogether literally turns EVERYTHING into extremely blocky textures.  DLSS is supposed to decrease your image quality in favor of AI upscaling and some more FPS. Here, you absolutely need to keep it turned on just to keep your game looking like it at least belongs in the 21st century. That is NOT what DLSS is supposed to do.

Aside from that, the game runs smoothly on 1440p and all max settings for me (with DLSS turned on for reasons stated above), but for some reason, I have absolutely MASSIVE input delay (2 to 3 seconds) despite my frame latency being relatively low (< 50 ms at all times). No matter what settings I change, the input delay stays the same. This isn't a frame latency issue, it's a game issue, and it makes the game completely unplayable. So yeah, I couldn't even tell you what updates they made to the actual game mechanics because the absolute fundamentals of the game are already so hopelessly broken to begin with.

tl;dr, as it is now, the remastered version of this game is a massive waste of your money. If you don't already have it, definitely do not buy it until they get their act together and fix this broken mess of a game.

comment:
I was positive I'd love this game, I mean look at the accolades and Steam rating.  I bought it once when it came out and got a refund.  Then, just this week I was convinced I just bought it at the wrong time the first time, and that now I'd really dig into it.

That didn't happen, I still think it is just plain overrated.  It has some positive aspects, not a complete waste of time but overall I just can't recommend it.  The main problem I have as a Keyboard and Mouse PC user is that the controls JUST PLAIN SUCK!  It's not just me, this is a  well known issue.  The target lock is broken, yes I know you can choose to not use it but let's be honest at this price and this far along in the game features that are in the game should just plain work.  This is what happens when a console title is ported to PC . . . poorly.  That alone is a deal breaker for me.

Another thing I just didn't care for are the enemies.  Not so much the bosses, but the regular enemies you encounter along the way.  They just seem so . . . "synthetic".  They remind me of automatons, like robots very strange looking and moving.  Yes the world is huge, but it seemed like I was just running around killing time looking for something useful to do, and at the  same time any threat that I came across was more than likely something that would just outright kill me.  The avatar you play in the game is just plain weak.  Not looking for easy mode here, I like a challenge but my "Hero" should have some better combat ability, especially when encountering enemies straight out of the gate in "newbie" areas.

The combat is pretty lame IMO, again mostly because of the horrendous controls and targeting.  Just kind of repetitive and uninteresting to me.  And the gear progression leaves not much to look forward to.  I start my Samurai with a weapon and armor set that I will be using pretty much the whole game.  Yes I can add +1, +2, +3, +4 to my Sword but wow, not much to look forward to or work for.  The armor I start with is pretty much it, and the Katana I start with is one of the best in game...so no progression to work towards there.

I'm certainly in the minority, as most folks LOVE this game.  But, I bought it once early on . . . got a refund.  Bought it again later on and walked away from it, again.  This time I had enough hours so that there was no refund option, so they got my money.

Bought Dark Souls II after uninstalling Elden Ring . . . WOW, now this is something special.  Wish I'd have bought this first!

comment:
Slightly hypocritical review, as I have enjoyed The Witcher 3 in the Next-Gen version, and I still will after downgrading from the Remastered version to Next-Gen with DX11 (Next-Gen and Classic are still available under the Beta branches).

But what CD Project Red and the gaming industry as a whole is doing with these graphical "upgrades" is madness.

I have spent hours tweaking the graphical settings for the game to look as good as it did in the Next-Gen update while maintaining solid 60 FPS, with mixed results. I can get it to run on 1440p@60 FPS with ultra/high settings and no Ray Tracing, but the problem is that it doesn't look good [i]consistently[/i].

This is because they have somehow introduced dynamic color pallets and lighting, so that the colors and illumination changes in different areas. Sometimes interiors are dark, sometimes a very bright gray. Sometimes it switches between looking good or bad as the colors and lighting changes from one frame to the other.

On top of that there are a tons of graphical glitches, popping, broken distant models, shadows, etc. And worst of all constant crashes, but I believe that this is a Linux/Proton issue that will be eventually fixed.

The "old" Next-Gen version in DX11 runs super super smooth and consistent with lots of headroom with my hardware. And it looks absolutely gorgeous!

What also shocks me is how many official reviews praise the update for the Path Tracing. I'm happy for everyone owning a 1.5k+ GPU, and Ray/Path Tracing are fascinating technologies, but personally think that the price of the hardware doesn't remotely justify these "enhancements". And it would be completely fine to have the options present in the game, but the fact that a 11 year old game becomes so badly optimized for modern mid-end hardware even with all the high-end stuff turned off is not acceptable!

Also some users do run the game with RT/PT, but then heavily rely on upscaling and frame generation. It surely is a matter of taste, but I find the looks too blurry with heavy upscaling and the delay too "floaty" with frame generation. And as I said before, I'm not even a fan of the new color palette/lighting, even with Path Tracing enabled. Summarized, the industry introduces super demanding graphical features to justify insanely expensive hardware, while introducing other technologies to downgrade the image/delay but boost the perceived FPS. And then they slap it onto old games, preventing them to run properly on modern, mid-range hardware.

As for the other new Remastered features, I will miss some of them. I especially like the additional accessibility features and quest markers on the map. Other than that I didn't notice the other improvements much.

I hope the Remastered version gets a lot more polish and optimization when the new DLC drops, so I can jump back into it and hopefully have a decent experience with a mid-range rig.

comment:
[h1] If you value roleplaying consistency, do not play this [/h1]

I've since dropped this game but I would appreciate it if someone would read through this and tell me where i may have gone wrong. Genuine advice would be appreciated. I want to like this game.

Consistency is not really something that you are going to find much of in this game. Its weird to talk about because often times these inconsistencies are intentional like the combat RNG (although intentional does not mean its good). What I want to focus on here in this review however is the consistency of the roleplaying aspect of the game and why I dont think its very good. What really irks me about this game is how said inconsistency in certain places does not translate well to the roleplaying aspect and general content of the game, if you want an RPG that respects your intent in a well polished and consistent manner, this is ABSOLUTELY not it despite the appearance it gives off of being able to do things however you possibly could want. One example of this that is not exclusive and in fact is the largest sign I personally found of a broader issue not just limited to combat in this game is the ability to fight people and cause chaos constantly. You can fight whoever you want and the game allows it and even encourages it as an intended and described approach during certain sidequests, however a good portion of the time, if you want to fight people, you will get curbstomped, and thus might have to rethink your approach and do something you didnt want to do for an outcome you didnt want. My issue is not born of difficulty, its born of the idea that if you want to be a hyper-aggressive gremlin, you are going to be punished for it a lot instead of rewarded and it can make it feel as if certain roleplaying options are not viable (again, not exclusive to fighting everyone), although being "rewarded" in this game is quite a subjective thing for many people. For a game as broad and inclusive towards literally everything as this, it really does not do a good job at integrating every possible way for players to go about things in an equal manner. In fact this exact thing is exactly what made me drop the game at the nere fight in act 1. I prepared as much as I possibly could think I could've, stabbed certain enemies in the back multiple times and save scummed in order to get optimal rolls on the damage values, and still couldnt get past the fight despite wanting to take the route of killing everyone and nere himself in that fight. Its wide as an ocean (everything you can do) but deep as a lake (the polish and value of each approach to a given situation). I dont expect every approach to be equally easy or equally rewarding, but I do expect the game to treat each playstyle it explicitly describes or offers as an equally viable and intentional way to play the game based on its presentation and it just does not manage that in my opinion. On a personal note: I am 35 hours in on one save slot and I have yet to figure out why people love this game so much, but I certainly know that at least for me, this game's unholy amounts of inconsistency in its combat, its tone, its outcomes and the inconsistency in the "RP" in "RPG" is just not for me. If you value roleplaying consistency and viability of your intentions in games, this is not what you are going to find here. Unless you've played D&D a lot in which case I can't really comment because I don't play D&D

Future edit: With a clear mind, I think there are some things I do genuinely believe are flaws, even with the months since I've played this. For one, when I say that your choices are not respected, that doesn't entirely mean just the dice screwing you over, but also the results of either succeeding or failing a roll. From what I remember, there really isnt anything that changes much when you succeed or fail a dialogue or skill check, the most things that happened for me were companions changing their opinions of you ever so slightly on an invisible scale (which given the amount of dialogue there is is basically worthless), the character fighting you which is just an extra hassle, or worst yet, content and options for your playthrough literally being locked out thanks to a dice roll and from what I could tell, absolutely nothing being done to balance out said locked content. Also, to expand on the combat, the best way I can describe it is switching between getting ♥♥♥♥♥♥ consensually and non-consensually by a 20 sided die CONSTANTLY. There are many encounters I walked into in the early game (most notably the goblin fight with dror ragzlin, the lycans attacking the cargo crew, and the nere fight), that are grossly overtuned for reasons I cant understand, these encounters kicked my ass multiple times and it was mostly because my party could not for the life of them get good rolls, and what makes it worse is that you could go a few feet away from them and fight something else that is much easier. Its overtuned fights in an area where they shouldn't be overtuned (I was playing on regular difficulty btw), on top of that, the enemies themselves also have an absurd amount of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ they can pull out of their ass whenever they want. In fact, what made me quit the game entirely was a moment in the nere fight when I had progressed through a good portion of it, but suddenly the enemies ensnare arrows start hitting perfectly every single time unlike before, and most notably, an enemy was throwing a bomb at my feet and the throw does 3/4 damage to the bomb, not quite enough to blow it up, however, in the last attempt I did, that same bomb randomly decided to take 4 damage and completely blow up my entire party for no reason. The combat is not only dictated by the dice, but also by swen vincke's wrath. Also, as for getting stronger, unfortunately this game does not do the best job at that. Here's the thing, at least in act 1, this game does not serve that well as an open world game, even in its more linear design as compared to something like breath of the wild. What I mean by this is that some sidequests will give you xp, some wont, some activities will give you xp, some wont, and some stuff you do literally wont give you so much as a weapon or item you'll never use. Compare this to something like elden ring where wherever you go, even if you get something worthless, you are still gathering runes for levels, in this game, you sometimes get ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. 
And onto my last point, the character writing is questionable. (Spoilers ahead) I know everyone loves this game's writing, but at least in act 1, there is nothing encouraging you to give a single flying ♥♥♥♥ about any of your companions save for wyll and karlach. Their entire development early game is them just telling you "I ♥♥♥♥♥♥ a goddess and wanted her love", "My society is very brutish and hardcore", "I am part of a religion that keeps secrets", "I am a vampire and I dont like it", it is simple character dialogue with nothing to show for it, like I have no reason to care, this is not a book where you have to use your mind to fill in the blanks and create an image, I am literally looking at these people and this world, why do I not get anything to show me why I should care. This is why I say wyll and karlach are the only 2 I actually gave a single ♥♥♥♥ about because with wyll, there's a scene where mizora will come down and literally sprout horns on his head in front of you, something he finds shameful, and with karlach, after you kill the paladins, she will take out her anger on the surrounding environment. This is show dont tell, and the rest of the companions dont get much of it at all. Also, to add to this, everyone, and I mean everyone is trying to jump your bones every chance they get in the early game to the point where it becomes a hassle trying to dodge having sex with someone constantly, the game continuously puts you in situations where it gives you a nudge nudge and a wink and I keep having to say "No".
