comment:
This is what happens when a very determined guy with a dream gets told "No" at one point in his life.
And responds with: "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ watch me."

Larian went a long way, and grew into a truly talented, experienced team. Divinity OS1-2 were their own little darlings and masterpieces. But BG3 just took it to a whole new level.

I... don't really see much point in going into depth with this review - the game already has 750k+ of overwhelmingly positive reviews. There's not much I can add here. The story is largely great, the characters are cool, memorable, and voice acting+motion capture is phenomenal. Graphics are great, soundtrack is epic, gameplay is DnD 5e, but much better suited for the nuances of a videogame, and much better balance. The amount of content and options for replayability is absurdly big. Easily a 9/10, and a well deserved GOTY.

The only peeves that I had with this game:
[list]
[*] You start as level 1, yet you're the "chosen ones" right off the bat, and you don't really feel level 1 narratively; only statistically. There's no sense of standard DnD party of strangers gathering up, meeting in some metaphorical tavern, getting slowly dragged into the maelstrom of events. No - you are immediately the chosen ones, everyone is super important, unique and powerful, with a backstory that fits a level 7-10 character AT LEAST.
[*] Most of your companions have a stupid thing in common - some super dark secret that they're uncomfortable sharing, but expect you to just be chill with it and trust them without giving you a proper explanation for a while.
[*] The game is definitely meant for a single player experience. Playing in coop is... just ruining most of the story. Unless you are roleplaying with your friends, then playing as a bunch of custom characters is a poor decision - you're just going to miss out on a whole bunch of content that you'll witness with a party of your NPC companions.
[*] I'm not sure if it got fixed over the years, but Act 3 really felt poorly optimized and most bugged at release. Can't speak for it's current state
[*] A bit of a spoiler, but not crucial one: [spoiler]Consuming tadpoles to increase your illithid powers has... virtually zero consequences. No effect on the ending, no actual effect on your relationship with your comrades (even if they verbally disapprove) [/spoiler], So refusing to use those powers does not reward you in any way, you just handicap yourself.
[/list]

comment: Not an elite gamer here. But i loved this game from the start to finish and would totally recommend it. The main story as well as the DLC were both good but unfortunately short. Yet each time the credits rolled (after each of the several endings you get to choose and play through), you are left with a sense of fulfillment, despite some of them being absolutely tragic. It is nothing but sheer brilliance from the game developers. I have played all the Witcher games which were developed by CDPR, and I think I will place CyberPunk above all of them, simply because of the level of reflection this game put me into accross several of its moments. There were still several bugs encountered throughout my playthrough but I didn't mind it at all. From what I have seen on the Internet about the game's disasterous launch, the game has come a long way. However, I don't think I'd return to NightCity anytime in the future (Personally I prefer to move on rather than dwell on the past in life), but the game is defintely worth replaying - each time with a different personality, a different combat style and different choice. So, yeah... 10/10.

comment:
Where do I even start with Baldur's Gate 3?

I've been playing D&D since I was around 11, so there was absolutely no way I was going to miss this game. I hadn't played the previous Baldur's Gate games, though, so BG3 was actually my introduction to the series. I got it as soon as it became available, and almost 1,000 hours later... apparently I'm still not done with it.

Achievements aren't really the focus for me here. I'm currently at 46/54, but BG3 is one of those games where I'd much rather start another character, try another choice and see where the story takes me than worry about completing a checklist.

The amount of freedom and variation is probably what I love most. Even after so many playthroughs, different interactions, consequences and unexpected outcomes can still appear. You make one seemingly insignificant choice differently and suddenly you're seeing something you've never seen before. It makes every run feel like its own D&D campaign rather than simply replaying the same story.

The modding possibilities make that experience even better. I love that the game can be modded so easily, although I've mostly kept mine to quality-of-life and graphical improvements. For me, it's about polishing and improving the experience without changing what makes the original game so good.

All three acts have something I love, although Act 2 is definitely my favourite. The atmosphere, the story and everything surrounding the Shadow-Cursed Lands just work incredibly well for me.

I love the companions too, although Gale, Astarion and Shadowheart have a special place among them. Gale takes first place when it comes to romance, though. ❤️

As for my own characters, Wizard is easily my favourite class and Drow my favourite race. Character creation gives you plenty to play around with, and combined with all the classes, subclasses, races, backgrounds, dialogue options and different ways of approaching situations, the replayability is enormous.

The story itself is great, but what really makes it special to me is how much it feels like *your* story. My most memorable Tav will probably always be my very first one, whom I played essentially as myself.

That adventure ended in Act 2 because I made a... let's call it a "wrong" decision.

The soundtrack deserves a mention as well. There are some beautiful tracks in there, and naturally, a few of them have found their way onto my Spotify playlists.

My main disappointment is knowing that development was, in some ways, rushed towards the end and that a number of things had to be cut. There are places where you can wonder what BG3 might have looked like if everything originally envisioned had made it into the finished game.

But even with that disappointment, what we got is still far more than excellent.

After 979.5 hours, countless characters, different decisions, romances, successes, catastrophes and apparently the occasional accidental premature ending, I'm still finding reasons to return to Baldur's Gate 3.

And I'm definitely not finished yet.

comment:
While Phantom Liberty was a great expansion, the update that was released alongside it absolutely ruined the game. 
They made all skill checks and areas scale with your character. The idea was to remove early level restrictions from the map and open up the entire city from the start. Which was just never a problem. The idea as a whole is just counterintuitive. It's basic game logic that the areas closer to big bads should be higher tier. And progressing towards them is half the fun of these types of open world games. Plus, it wasn't like leveling to keep up while exploring was remotely difficult or problematic in any way.
This change wasn't just unnecessary, it also ruins the experience as a whole. Your character now feels less competent the more you level, actively punishing you for exploration, and it restricts your character building by FORCING you into specialized builds.
Now this can be fixed with a mod and the game is still great otherwise, but I could never recommend a game that requires a mod to feel playable. 

TLDR: 2.0 ruined the game by punishing exploration and forcing character specialization, this is fixable through mods, but screw the developers for doing this to begin with.

comment:
Cyberpunk 2077 is a great game, and the story is amazing. Personally, I really liked playing as male V.
It is sad because this game had so much potential, but CD Projekt Red did not develop many parts of the world enough. For example, driving could be better, there could have been flying cars, more stores you can actually enter, and more NPCs with different voices and animations.
When you leave the main storyline and just explore the city, the game can still feel empty. It has improved compared to before, but I expected much more. The physics, cars, NPCs, and animations can still be very buggy and sometimes do not feel smooth. It is disappointing that even after almost six years, some of these problems are still there.
I think Cyberpunk 2077 could have been one of the greatest games of all time if it had received another five or six years of development, but CD Projekt Red made the choice to release it when they did.
The game is still worth playing and finishing, especially for the main story. The Dogtown/Phantom Liberty storyline is also very good. But if you like exploring the open world and paying attention to small details, you will notice many of the game's weaknesses.
I finished the game, experienced all the endings, and completed all the achievements. My favorite ending is “(Don't Fear) The Reaper.” I really enjoyed the idea of V and Johnny deciding to attack Arasaka Tower alone instead of risking the lives of their friends.
Even with all its problems, I recommend Cyberpunk 2077

comment:
The dialogues are moronic. Most characters just trauma dump you every chance they get. Talking about mind-numbingly boring life stories... Like dude, I steal and murder for you, IDGAF about your poor upbringing or your past partners. Most people that are supposed to be the good guys are awful. I've tried to kill so many of them, especially Panam (I hate that childish, ret****d b**ch with passion), but sadly there's no player choice in that regard... Even Starfield at least allows you to hurt and down essential NPCs and make enemies. Let me repeat - THE ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ SLOPFIELD!

I was under impression that players could influence who V becomes, but outside of customizing your character at the beginning of the game, the story feels ridiculously linear. Lots of "choices" where V says the same thing in a different way. V is V, just like Geralt is Geralt in the Witcher games, and you can't do anything beyond that, but to play as the devs wrote them.

RPG mechanics are almost non existent. Life path you choose have almost 0 impact on the game. Dialogue options are comically limited to the point where Fallout 4 system feels deep. And that's a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ impressive achievement.

20h into the game my character was already an unkillable god on the highest difficulty. Action mechanics are all-right, although since the game is so easy and boring it doesn't really matter.

The amount of girl bosses that are boasting and talking ♥♥♥♥ to you is staggering. And the fact that you just can't shut them up (unlike male characters who do the same), or stand up for yourself in any capacity really bothers me and takes away immersion from this supposed "RPG". When I saw ms. President acting all tuff like some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ commando and talking down to V who JUST RESCUED HER I was genuinely laughing out loud. And the only dialogue options you have with her are essentially "Yes Queen. Lead the way my Queen". No wonder this world is such a mess with leaders like that.

The only thing that kept me playing is the Night City. Hands down the best open world I've ever seen. Yet despite that, most of the time spent in this game I was thinking about playing Deus Ex or GTA 4 again for god know which time.

Soundtrack is great too.

And the fact that they've dropped their awesome and beautiful engine for UE5 is the funniest news I've seen this decade.

comment:
If you've never played a Dark Souls, Demon's Souls, or even Bloodborne, starting here is okay. I recommend this game to anyone who has never played a FromSoftware game before. But if you've already played their previous games AND you're hoping to encounter something new, sadly, this is not the case.

The game literally recycles animations, items, attacks, enemies, and mechanics from its past games. Same animations, same attacks, same items, all with subtle reworks to item images and slightly different animations, but underneath, it's the same. I played the previous FromSoftware games and liked them, but I can't ignore that this feels like the same game.

In fact, this game could be called Dark Souls 4, and I'd be okay with it, because that's what it is: Dark Souls with mods.

Btw, I know Demon's Souls came first, but the same lineage is there: Demon's Souls, Bloodborne, Dark Souls, and now Elden Ring. The only game that really escaped this pattern is Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice, which actually changed things.

If you look at FromSoftware's games over time, you can see a pattern. They take what they already did, adjust it, and try to perfect the formula, but they don't create enough new things. Look at Armored Core and Frame Gride, for example. It's the same idea, trying to perfect the formula, and then they continue with Armored Core and Another Century's Episode.

I don't care if they reuse elements from past games, but do you know who does this too? Activision with Call of Duty.

And look, Elden Ring is fun, but there are a lot of things that feel like Bandai Namco the publisher, not the developer put its hands on parts of the game. I remember playing Code Vein, the typical Souls like that tries to be unique but ends up feeling like, "Hey, look, I'm Dark Souls too." It was disappointing, with its vague story and some parts like The Depths: Tower of Trials, where the enemy damage made no sense.

Elden Ring also starts with static images instead of the kind of cinematics that gave context at the beginning of Dark Souls, Sekiro, or Bloodborne. I remember thinking, "Wow, wait a second." There are things in Elden Ring that feel like they were just written into the script because yes.

The Fire Giant is a good example. You're close to the end of the game, there is no cinematic and barely any context, and when you reach him, the fight doesn't feel special. Remember Dark Souls III and Yhorm the Giant? If you did Siegward of Catarina's quest, he appeared there, and suddenly the fight had more context and feeling. It felt like you had to finish something.

In Elden Ring, the Fire Giant feels like a boss placed there just to fill an empty, soulless scenario.

The game also has too many bosses. You enter a cave, explore for a while, suddenly a health bar appears, "epic" music starts, and you fight another boss. Then you do it again. Because it happens so often, bosses stop feeling special.

Even the main bosses were a disappointing experience for me. There is so much recycling. Look at Margit, the Fell Omen. I saw that guy like three times, or maybe it was Morgott, the Omen King, because they all look the same. Down in Leyndell, Royal Capital, there is also an illusion that is basically a copy of Margit or Morgott. Even Godrick the Grafted didn't feel that unique to me.

Radahn was also disappointing. Only in the DLC do you really see his power. I understand that the version we fight in the base game is weakened, but still, we're fighting this legendary warrior while he's riding a skinny, scrawny horse.

Malenia, however, actually felt special. She was fun. And the final Marika/Radagon encounter was cool because it felt like the game was telling me, "I'm the Elden Ring." Not me saying it the boss itself felt like it was saying that.

Godfrey was also disappointing. I expected a real version of the Elden Lord, something like when you fight Gwyn or even the Soul of Cinder. Not because I wanted a harder fight, but because of the feeling you get when you fight them for the first time. Godfrey didn't give me that feeling. He felt weak.

And then there is co-op. I bought this game expecting to play with friends, but if you want to play with friends, forget it or at least, that's how it felt to me. You get invaded constantly, and it becomes annoying when you're just trying to explore.

In past games, invasions had a purpose. You could farm items for the covenant you joined and get special rewards, like Darkmoon Blade from the Blade of the Darkmoon. In Elden Ring, that doesn't exist in the same way. Invading other players often feels like PvP for no reason.

And you already have THREE different arenas for PvP. Some people prefer invading because they enjoy it, and that's fine, but from my experience, getting invaded while trying to explore with friends made no sense.

So don't expect to easily play through the whole game with friends. I ended up playing almost the entire game alone, even though I bought it expecting to play with them, and eventually they just left the game because of things like this.

I'm also worried about the direction FromSoftware is taking. This "new DLC" attitude of "it's just $5" makes me worry that in the future the company could become like Activision, Bethesda, or Ubisoft. I really hope that never happens.

And then you see the new FromSoftware game coming to Nintendo Switch another Souls game, or basically Bloodborne with jumps. Do you see the pattern? The direction they're taking? Maybe I'm wrong. I hope I am.

So, who is Elden Ring for?

If you've never played a FromSoftware game: play it. It's fun, huge, challenging, and has an incredible amount of content.

If you've already played their previous games and you want more of the same formula, you'll probably like it.

But if you've played them all and you're hoping to find something genuinely new, think about it before buying. Maybe you won't care that it's the same formula. Maybe you'll love it anyway. But maybe, like me, you'll regret the purchase.

When I watched the trailers and gameplay, I had this feeling in the back of my head saying, "Hey, this is the same game as the past FromSoftware games." And literally, it was.

I wasn't wrong.

Dark Souls 4 with mods.

comment:
TL;DR

An incredible genre defining souls-like experience for returning veterans and new players to the genre like myself. The soundtrack transports you to another world and the beautifully crafted open environments keep the feelings of discovery and wonder riding high past the story's conclusion. All the same can be said about the DLC, sometimes feeling like an entirely new game with its new systems and ideas. This is easily in my top 5, probably even top 3 games of all time. If you haven't played a souls-like game before and are looking for where to start, start here. You won't regret it. It's time to get gud. 

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

I finally understand what the hype was all about. I didn't play the game until many years after its release. It was my first souls-like game and while it took me time to learn the mechanics, it was extremely rewarding in every aspect. The build crafting, open world, different endings, combat, soundtrack; the list goes on and on. It might have the best soundtrack I have ever heard in a videogame. It was so good I had to replay it again with a different build after my first playthrough. I heard some complain of lack of story, but this one critique that repeatedly kept me invested. It reminded me of the saying, “show, don't tell” because the game lets you piece many story beats together through your own imagination and experiences with the world. I say this but if you really care enough, there’s plenty of story lines here through character interactions, quests, and bosses. Somehow after completing this game almost a year ago I STILL find videos online of quests, bosses, or weapons I never knew existed in the world. That sense of wonder and fantasy is what makes you want to come back and play even after replaying the game numerous times. Upon writing this, I might just go back and replay the game again. It’s just that good.

comment:
130 gigabyte game that runs terribly on high-end devices.

The scope of the game is as impressive as it is ambitious; however, the combat system and the way in which the game feels to navigate makes for a grating, miserable experience, no matter how good or bad the decisions are that you make.
Even on the regular difficulty, enemies will constantly use the terrain and their vast understanding of the niche inner workings of combat to put the player(s) in lose-lose situations.
Story moments being locked by default for player characters who are unconscious was another glaring downside.
Why in the world would the level 17 dragon in the grand-scale final battle be less of a problem than the infinite magic missiles being sent out 
God forbid you want to pick any of the non-damaging spells that require any sort of creativity to use; the game punishes you heavily for not min-maxing your build to deal as much damage as possible, no exceptions. It does not help that the enemy always seems to know your next move and will make your time as miserable as possible within what they are capable of doing, having access to an infinite number of spell slots and class actions at their disposal. 

The most damning aspect was that the payoff for it all -- for 280+ hours of gameplay and half a dozen false starts with different groups of friends to get a game together -- is that the ending feels empty. The entire party can just fail checks and miss pretty significant context for the story as a whole.
It feels as if the multiplayer aspect of the game was tacked on at the very end; This Game Was Not Built For Muiltple People To Play It At Once.


It's probably a good game and fun experience if you have no friends.

comment:
A great D&D adaptation, but a frustrating game

Baldur’s Gate 3 does an impressive job of translating D&D rules into a video game. Character classes, spells, abilities, dice rolls and many other mechanics are remarkably well implemented.

Unfortunately, I increasingly dislike the actual game built around those mechanics.

The biggest problem is the combat design. Especially in Act 3, major encounters constantly introduce enemies with special abilities that are poorly explained or completely unexpected. Enemies become invisible, stun characters, move without provoking opportunity attacks, apply multiple status effects, create darkness, and use combinations of actions that are difficult to understand from the player's perspective.

The problem isn't difficulty. **The problem is a lack of information.**

A good D&D encounter gives you enough information to make tactical decisions. BG3 too often makes you discover the rules by getting hit by them first. Eventually combat starts feeling less like *“How do I outsmart these enemies?”* and more like *“What ridiculous special ability did the game just pull out of nowhere?”*

Large encounters are another problem. Watching 15–20 enemies take their turns one after another makes fights incredibly slow. Combine that with all the status effects, animations and special abilities, and some battles become an exhausting exercise in waiting.

The camp system also becomes increasingly annoying. Wanting to take a long rest can turn into another cutscene, companion conversation, romance scene, dream sequence or even a fight. The companions are interesting, but the game sometimes feels like **group therapy with occasional adventuring in between**.

Loot has the opposite problem. In BG1 and BG2, finding a magical item was exciting. In Act 3 of BG3, I constantly find supposedly powerful items and think: *“What am I supposed to do with this?”* Many are so build-specific that they immediately become vendor trash.

And then there are the technical and UI problems: unclear mechanics, missing or misleading indicators, awkward camera behavior, and situations where the game behaves differently from what its descriptions suggest.

I actually like the D&D rules in BG3 a lot.

**It's the game built around them that increasingly frustrates me.**

I enjoyed BG1, BG2, Icewind Dale and Neverwinter Nights much more. They had fewer systems, smaller encounters and less spectacle, but they generally **let me play instead of constantly getting in my way**.

At this point, I frequently find myself asking:

**“How do I beat this?”**

followed by:

**“Do I really want to spend another hour doing this?”**

That's a disappointing place for a Baldur's Gate game to leave me.

**Excellent D&D implementation. Increasingly frustrating game design.**
